The oral tradition was important in pre-modern literature because it allowed stories, legends, myths and other types of literature to be passed down from generation to generation through spoken word rather than written down.
The oral tradition was used to communicate important cultural and historical information to a wider audience.
The oral tradition helped to preserve and transmit cultural heritage, values, and beliefs.

Beowulf was preserved through oral tradition for centuries before being written down.
The Iliad and The Odyssey were originally passed down through oral tradition before being written down.
The Mahabharata was mostly passed down through oral tradition before being written down.
The Aboriginal Dreamtime stories were passed down orally for tens of thousands of years before being recorded in writing.
There are downsides to relying solely on oral tradition for preserving literature, including the possibility of losing or distorting information over time due to the fallibility of memory.
Different storytellers may interpret and retell the story in their own ways, leading to variations or contradictions in the tale's details.
It can be harder to maintain the original language of the story when it's passed on orally, as the spoken word is more fluid than the written word.
Oral traditions can be susceptible to being lost altogether due to the passing of generations.
